## Purpose

This document synthesizes the main hypotheses tested in the FCFS clinic appointment simulation. The focus is on how class-specific properties affect access, utilization, delay, balking, and class advantage.

Each hypothesis is assigned a concise verdict: `Supported`, `Supported (condition)`, `Qualified`, or `Not supported`. `Qualified` means the mechanism is present, but the broad version of the claim would be misleading without specifying the relevant denominator, timing, or regime. Sweeps are done with all other baseline assumptions fixed, with each step repeated across 100 seeds.

## Metric Interpretation

Under oversubscription, utilization is not an access metric by itself: served rate is the primary aggregate access metric. Offered wait must be reported with no-offer share because patients who receive no offer have no wait observation, while accepted wait is selected by balking. These metrics should therefore be read together rather than treated as interchangeable summaries.

## H1 Evidence: Class 1 Cancellation Sweep {#h1-cancellation-evidence}

This sweep varies only Class 1's cancellation probability while holding Class 2 at the baseline cancellation probability of 0.10.

The hypothesis is supported if higher Class 1 cancellation probability lowers offered delay under high demand, lowers Class 1's own served rate, and reallocates some completed visits to Class 2.

### Mean Offered Booking Delay

![Mean offered booking delay by class](../../../outputs/class1_cancellation/figures/mean_offered_delay_by_class.png)

This figure tests whether higher Class 1 cancellation probability shortens offered delay. In the sweep, mean offered delay falls from about 11.84 days to about 7.47 days as Class 1 cancellation probability rises from 0.00 to 0.30. This is consistent with future cancellations reopening slots that the pooled FCFS queue can offer to later arrivals under high demand.

### Served Rate

![Served rate by class](../../../outputs/class1_cancellation/figures/percent_serviced_by_class.png)

This figure tests whether higher Class 1 cancellation probability lowers Class 1's own served rate. Class 1 served rate falls from about 0.344 to about 0.175, while Class 2 served rate rises from about 0.135 to about 0.395. A cancellation can improve calendar flexibility for the pool while still harming the class whose appointments are being canceled.

### Average Utilization and Class Slot Shares

![Average utilization and class slot shares](../../../outputs/class1_cancellation/figures/average_utilization_aggregate.png)

This figure tests whether future cancellations are recycled into completed visits. If aggregate utilization stays flat or rises, then cancellations are not simply wasting capacity under this stress-test regime; they are reopening future slots that can be rebooked.

### H1 Conclusion

H1 is supported. The evidence supports a high-demand reallocation mechanism: the canceling class loses access, and other patients may gain nearer slots. The overclaim to avoid is that cancellations are good for clinic access as a general recommendation.

## H2 Evidence: Balking Step × Arrival Rate {#h2-balking-arrival-evidence}

This sweep varies both the high-balking probability (0.0–0.9) and the per-class arrival rate (λ = 20, 35, 50, 65) symmetrically across both classes. The goal is to test whether balking step's effect on mean offered booking delay changes direction under different demand regimes.

The hypothesis is supported if (1) offered delay is unaffected by balking at low demand, (2) offered delay decreases monotonically at moderate demand, and (3) offered delay initially rises before falling at high demand.

### Mean Offered Booking Delay by Arrival Rate

![Offered delay by arrival rate](../../../outputs/balking_step_by_arrival/figures/offered_delay_by_arrival_rate.png)

At low demand (λ/S = 1.25), offered delay is flat at approximately 3.1 days regardless of balking step — the calendar is never congested, so balking has nothing to relieve. At moderate demand (λ/S = 2.19), offered delay falls monotonically from approximately 9.1 to 7.5 days as balking removes enough demand to ease congestion.

At high demand (λ/S ≥ 3.12), offered delay rises at low-to-moderate balking before eventually falling. The mechanism: moderate balking reduces the no-offer rate, converting patients who previously received no offer into patients who receive long-delay offers. These new long-delay offers pull the average up. Only at high balking does total demand drop enough to genuinely shorten the calendar. The higher the demand, the more persistent this hump.

### H2 Conclusion

H2 is supported. The same patient behavior produces opposite effects on the same metric depending on demand pressure. Under the stress-test baseline (λ/S = 3.12), moderate balking paradoxically worsens offered delay before improving it — a pattern absent at lower demand levels. This means balking's impact on offered delay cannot be generalized without specifying the demand regime.

[Back to summary table](#summary-table)


## H3 Evidence: Balking Selection Effect {#h3-balking-selection-evidence}

This sweep varies Class 1's high-balking probability (0.0–0.9) while holding Class 2 at baseline. The hypothesis is supported if accepted delay drops while offered delay stays flat or rises — proving the delay improvement is selection, not reduced congestion.

### Offered Delay vs. Accepted Delay

![Mean offered booking delay](../../../outputs/class1_balking/figures/mean_offered_delay_by_class.png)

![Mean accepted booking delay](../../../outputs/class1_balking/figures/mean_accepted_delay_by_class.png)

Offered delay stays flat or rises slightly across the sweep (from approximately 9.9 to 10.1 at moderate balking, then falling to approximately 8.4 at 0.9). Accepted delay drops steadily from approximately 9.9 to 6.6 for Class 1. The two metrics diverge because higher balking removes the long-wait patients from the accepted sample without relieving congestion on the calendar. By contrast, the H1 cancellation sweep shows both metrics falling in lockstep — a genuine congestion reduction.

### H3 Conclusion

H3 is qualified. At low-to-moderate balking, the accepted delay drop is primarily a selection artifact — offered delay stays flat or rises while accepted delay falls. At high balking (above 0.5), offered delay also begins to fall, indicating genuine congestion relief contributes alongside selection. Accepted delay remains an unreliable congestion signal when balking is present, but the effect is not purely selection at all levels.

[Back to summary table](#summary-table)


## H4 Evidence: Balking vs. No-Show Loss {#h4-balking-vs-no-show-evidence}

The comparison is best interpreted as a timing mechanism. Balking happens before booking and consumes no slot. Cancellation releases future booked slots before the service day and can be rebooked. No-show occurs on the service day and cannot be rebooked.

The hypothesis is supported if the Class 1 balking sweep shows relatively stable aggregate utilization despite declining Class 1 served rate, while the Class 1 no-show sweep shows declining aggregate utilization and declining Class 1 served rate.

### Loss Timing Comparison

![H4 loss timing comparison](../../../outputs/h4_balking_vs_noshow/figures/h4_loss_timing_comparison.png)

The left panel overlays overall utilization from both sweeps. Balking (purple) holds flat at approximately 0.84 across the full 0.0–0.9 range, while no-show (green) falls from approximately 0.92 to 0.68. Pre-booking losses consume no slot and are absorbed by other patients in the FCFS queue; service-day losses waste booked slots that cannot be rebooked.

The right panel overlays Class 1 served rate from both sweeps. Both lines decline, confirming that the affected class loses access regardless of when the loss occurs. No-show losses produce a steeper decline because the patient occupies a slot through booking but fails to convert it into a completed visit.

### H4 Conclusion

H4 is supported. The evidence supports the timing distinction: balking is pre-booking, cancellation is future-slot release, and no-show is service-day loss. This interpretation applies under the current implementation; the overclaim to avoid is treating all loss channels as if they had the same capacity consequence.

[Back to summary table](#summary-table)

## H5 Evidence: Symmetric FCFS and Arrival Share {#h5-symmetric-fcfs-and-arrival-share}

The controlled symmetric arrival-share experiment shows that varying Class 1's share does not create a meaningful per-arrival class access gap when behavioral parameters are symmetric. The gap stays around -0.002 to +0.002 as Class 1 share varies from 0.30 to 0.70. This supports the interpretation that pooled FCFS is neutral under symmetric behavior, and that observed class gaps require behavioral asymmetry or interaction effects.

[Back to summary table](#summary-table)

## H6 Evidence: Driver Ranking and Local Attribution {#h6-driver-ranking-and-local-attribution}

The broad regression screen and the realistic attribution experiment answer different questions. The regression screen ranks associations across a sampled design space, while the attribution experiment decomposes one realistic scenario. In the local attribution output, the full gap is about 0.213, with about 0.120 from no-show asymmetry, 0.073 from cancellation, and 0.019 from balking threshold. The relevant conclusion is therefore not that one driver universally dominates, but that class-gap driver rankings are regime-specific.

Booking horizon acts as a design modifier: in the realistic parameterization, it can amplify the class gap until roughly a three-week horizon, after which the effect plateaus.

[Back to summary table](#summary-table)

**Interpretation Across Mechanisms.** Cancellation is best read as high-demand reallocation, no-show loss as regime-dependent service-day loss, balking as accepted-wait selection plus class reallocation, and arrival share alone as insufficient to create a class access gap under symmetric behavior.

## Conclusion

This synthesis sharpens the interpretation along three dimensions. First, the denominator matters: utilization, served rate, offered wait, accepted wait, and no-offer share answer different questions. Second, timing matters: balking, cancellation, and no-show occur at different points in the booking process and therefore have different capacity consequences. Third, regime matters: no-show effects and class-gap driver rankings depend on demand pressure, threshold placement, and parameterization.


## H7 Evidence: Balking Level vs. Class Difference {#h7-balking-gap-vs-level-evidence}

This hypothesis asks whether class differences in outcomes are driven more by the absolute level of balking or by the difference between Class 1 and Class 2 balking behavior.

The hypothesis is supported if class gaps remain small when Class 1 and Class 2 have similar balking steps, but become larger when one class has a higher balking step than the other.

### Balking Step: Class 1 Access Advantage

![Balking step class advantage](../metric_analysis/figures/balking_step_benefit_heatmaps.png)

The main evidence is the Class 1 access-advantage panel. The diagonal band is close to neutral, meaning that when Class 1 and Class 2 have similar balking steps, neither class has a large served-rate advantage. Away from the diagonal, the class gap becomes stronger. When Class 1's balking step is higher than Class 2's, Class 1 loses access relative to Class 2. When Class 2's balking step is higher, Class 1 gains access relative to Class 2.

This pattern suggests that class advantage is driven mainly by the relative difference between the two classes' balking behavior, not simply by the absolute level of balking in the system.

### H7 Conclusion

H7 is supported. The class-advantage pattern is clearest off the diagonal, where the two classes have different balking steps. Along the diagonal, where both classes have similar balking behavior, class gaps remain small even when the absolute balking level changes.

This means that symmetric balking changes mostly affect the shared booking environment, while unequal balking behavior shifts access between classes.

[Back to summary table](#summary-table)


## H8 Evidence: No-Show Level vs. Class Difference {#h8-no-show-level-vs-gap-evidence}

This hypothesis asks whether no-show outcomes are driven more by the absolute no-show level or by the difference between Class 1 and Class 2 no-show behavior.

The key distinction is:

- absolute level: both classes have similarly high or low no-show risk;
- relative difference: one class has higher no-show risk than the other.

The hypothesis is supported if aggregate utilization changes when both classes' no-show levels rise together, while class access advantage changes most strongly when one class has higher no-show risk than the other.

### No-Show Step: Aggregate Utilization and Class Advantage

![No-show step benefit heatmaps](../metric_analysis/figures/no_show_step_benefit_heatmaps.png)

This figure provides the main evidence for H8. The utilization panel should be read as the absolute-level effect: when no-show risk is high for both classes, more booked appointments fail to become completed visits, so aggregate utilization falls.

The class-advantage panel should be read as the relative-difference effect. Along the diagonal, where Class 1 and Class 2 have similar no-show steps, class advantage should remain close to neutral even if the absolute no-show level changes. Away from the diagonal, class advantage becomes stronger because one class loses more completed visits than the other.

### No-Show Step: Class Gap

![No-show step class gap heatmap](../metric_analysis/figures/no_show_step_interaction_heatmap.png)

This figure isolates the class-gap interpretation. If Class 1 has a higher no-show step than Class 2, Class 1 should have a lower served rate relative to Class 2. If Class 2 has a higher no-show step, the direction should reverse.

This supports the claim that class differences are driven by relative differences in no-show behavior, not simply by the absolute level of no-shows in the system.

### H8 Conclusion

H8 is supported. Absolute no-show levels matter most for aggregate utilization because no-show slots are lost on the service day and cannot be rebooked. Relative no-show differences matter most for class access advantage because the class with higher no-show risk loses more completed visits relative to the other class.

In short, the average no-show level explains the system-level loss, while the no-show gap explains which class is disadvantaged.

[Back to summary table](#summary-table)


## H9 Evidence: Balking Threshold Crossing a High-Mass Delay Region {#h9-balking-threshold-evidence}

This hypothesis tests whether balking-threshold effects are smooth or nonlinear. The key idea is that threshold changes matter more when they cross delay regions where many patients are being offered or accepting appointments.

The hypothesis is partially supported. The evidence shows that threshold changes have stronger effects in the late part of the booking horizon, but it does not isolate `tau ≈ 11` as the unique point where the largest jump occurs.

### Baseline Accepted Booking Delay Distribution

![Baseline accepted booking delay distribution](../../../outputs/class1_balking_threshold/figures/accepted_delay_distribution_baseline.png)

This figure shows where accepted bookings are concentrated under the baseline balking threshold. The mass around later booking delays, including `tau ≈ 11`, suggests that threshold changes in this region can affect many patients.

However, this figure is only a baseline diagnostic. It does not show the accepted-delay distribution under every threshold value in the sweep. Once the balking threshold changes, Class 1 accepts and rejects different offers, which changes the future booking calendar and can shift the accepted-delay distribution.

### Accepted Booking Delay Distribution at Threshold 10

![Accepted booking delay distribution at threshold 10](../../../outputs/class1_balking_threshold/figures/accepted_delay_distribution_threshold10.png)

This figure checks whether the accepted-delay distribution remains the same after the Class 1 balking threshold changes. If the mass around `tau ≈ 11` changes, then the baseline histogram should not be treated as a fixed explanation for the threshold-sweep jumps.

This matters because the threshold sweep reruns the whole simulation at each threshold. It does not simply reclassify one fixed baseline group. Each threshold changes the booking calendar, which changes which delays later patients are offered and which delays appear in the accepted sample.

### Balking Rate

![Balking rate by class](../../../outputs/class1_balking_threshold/figures/balking_rate_by_class.png)

This figure tests the direct behavioral effect of the threshold change. Class 1's balking rate decreases as the threshold rises because fewer offered delays fall into the high-balking region.

The graph supports the claim that threshold effects are nonlinear in the late-horizon region. However, the largest change is not uniquely tied to crossing `tau ≈ 11`. This weakens the stronger version of the hypothesis that a single popular booking day mechanically produces the largest jump.

### Mean Accepted Booking Delay

![Mean accepted booking delay by class](../../../outputs/class1_balking_threshold/figures/mean_accepted_delay_by_class.png)

This figure shows how the accepted patient sample changes as the threshold rises. When Class 1 becomes willing to accept longer-delay offers, more long-delay patients remain in the accepted sample, raising Class 1's mean accepted booking delay.

The changes are consistent with nonlinear threshold behavior, but they do not show that the jump at `tau ≈ 11` is uniquely larger than nearby threshold changes.

### Served Rate

![Served rate by class](../../../outputs/class1_balking_threshold/figures/percent_serviced_by_class.png)

This figure tests whether the threshold effect reaches access outcomes, not only delay composition. As Class 1's threshold rises, Class 1 becomes more willing to accept long-delay appointments, which can increase its served rate and shift access away from Class 2.

The served-rate evidence supports the broader idea that threshold changes affect class outcomes, but it does not isolate `tau ≈ 11` as the only decisive crossing point.

### H9 Conclusion

H9 is partially supported. The evidence supports the broader claim that balking-threshold effects are nonlinear when the threshold moves through the late-horizon booking region. The accepted-delay histograms show that the system has substantial booking mass in this region, and the threshold-sweep graphs show nonlinear changes in balking rate, accepted delay, and served rate.

However, the evidence does not fully support the narrower claim that crossing `tau ≈ 11` specifically produces the largest jump. The baseline accepted-delay distribution changes when the threshold changes, and the largest metric changes may occur at nearby late-horizon thresholds. Therefore, the hypothesis is best interpreted as evidence of late-horizon nonlinear threshold effects, not as proof that `tau ≈ 11` is uniquely decisive.

![Research note main panel](../metric_analysis/figures/research_note_main_panel.png)

[Back to summary table](#summary-table)

## H10 Evidence: Class 1 No-Show Sweep {#h10-no-show-evidence}

This sweep varies only Class 1's high-delay no-show probability while holding Class 2 at baseline.

The hypothesis is supported if higher Class 1 no-show probability reduces completed visits when no-shows occur, while the size of the utilization effect depends on whether the regime creates enough no-show-risk exposure.

### Average Utilization and Class Slot Shares

![Average utilization and class slot shares](../../../outputs/class1_no_show/figures/average_utilization_aggregate.png)

As Class 1's high no-show probability rises, Class 1 contributes fewer completed visits. Because no-show slots are not rebooked under the current implementation, those losses directly reduce completed slots. In the stress-test no-show sweep, utilization falls from about 0.920 to about 0.681.

### Served Rate

![Served rate by class](../../../outputs/class1_no_show/figures/percent_serviced_by_class.png)

This figure shows that higher no-show risk lowers Class 1's served rate. The loss is direct because a booked appointment reaches the service day but does not become a completed visit.

### Mean Offered Booking Delay

![Mean offered booking delay by class](../../../outputs/class1_no_show/figures/mean_offered_delay_by_class.png)

This figure tests whether higher no-show risk improves delay. A flat offered-delay curve supports the view that no-shows are mainly a completion loss rather than a congestion-relief mechanism.

### Balking Rate

![Balking rate by class](../../../outputs/class1_no_show/figures/balking_rate_by_class.png)

This figure shows the no-show increase is not producing an offsetting benefit through fewer rejected offers.

### H10 Conclusion

H2 is supported. No-shows are unrebookable service-day losses under the current implementation, but the utilization effect is regime-dependent. In the realistic demand/no-show grid at lambda/S = 1.2, doubling no-show intensity changes utilization only from about 0.935 to about 0.934. The overclaim to avoid is that no-show risk has the same aggregate effect in every demand regime; threshold ordering and demand gating belong inside this hypothesis.

## H11 Evidence: Pre-Threshold vs. Post-Threshold Balking Rate {#h11-pre-vs-post-threshold-evidence}

This experiment tests whether the location of a between-class balking rate difference — below or above the threshold — affects the served-rate gap. Both scenarios hold the gap magnitude at 0.30, the Class 2 step size at 0.20, and Class 1 parameters fixed at b₀=0.00, b₁=0.50. Only the placement of the 0.30 between-class difference changes.

| Scenario | Class 1 (b₀, b₁) | Class 2 (b₀, b₁) | Gap location |
|----------|-------------------|-------------------|--------------|
| A        | (0.00, 0.50)      | (0.30, 0.50)      | Pre-threshold |
| B        | (0.00, 0.50)      | (0.00, 0.20)      | Post-threshold |

The hypothesis is supported if Scenario A produces a larger served-rate gap than Scenario B.

### Served-Rate Gap Comparison

![Pre vs. post threshold comparison](../../../outputs/pre_vs_post_threshold/figures/pre_vs_post_comparison.png)

Scenario A (pre-threshold gap) produces a served-rate gap of 0.065. Scenario B (post-threshold gap) produces 0.038. The pre-threshold difference has approximately 1.7 times more impact on the class gap, despite identical gap magnitude and step size. This follows from the delay distribution: pre-threshold balking acts on all patients offered delays 1 through 9, which accounts for roughly half of all offers. Post-threshold balking only acts on the subset offered delays above 9.

### H11 Conclusion

H11 is supported. With all other parameters controlled, placing a between-class balking difference below the threshold produces a larger served-rate gap than placing it above. Pre-threshold balking has wider population exposure and therefore greater impact on class-level outcomes.

[Back to summary table](#summary-table)

## H12 Evidence: Step Size vs. Post-Threshold Level {#h12-step-vs-level-evidence}

This experiment isolates two factors that determine a class's balking behavior: the within-class step size (b₁ − b₀) and the absolute post-threshold level (b₁). Two controlled sweeps vary one factor while holding the other constant, both applied to Class 1 with Class 2 at baseline.

| Sweep | Fixed factor | Varied factor | How it varies |
|-------|-------------|---------------|---------------|
| Purple | Step = 0.30 | Post-threshold (b₁) | b₁ rises from 0.30 to 0.70; b₀ rises with it (0.00 to 0.40) to maintain the fixed step |
| Green | Post-threshold (b₁) = 0.50 | Step (b₁ − b₀) | b₀ decreases from 0.40 to 0.00, widening the step from 0.10 to 0.50 |

The hypothesis is supported if the post-threshold sweep produces a larger swing in Class 1 served rate than the step-size sweep. In the green sweep, increasing the step means lowering b₀ — so a larger step corresponds to less pre-threshold balking, which improves served rate.

### Class 1 Served Rate Comparison

![Step vs. post-threshold level](../../../outputs/step_vs_post_level/figures/step_vs_post_level.png)

The post-threshold sweep (purple) produces a served-rate swing of 0.083 (from 0.284 down to 0.201). The step-size sweep (green) produces a swing of 0.048 (from 0.221 up to 0.269). Per unit change, the post-threshold level has approximately 1.7 times more impact on served rate than step size. This follows from the delay distribution: post-threshold balking governs the τ ≈ 10–12 region where roughly 55% of bookings concentrate, giving it more leverage than the pre-threshold rate which acts on the flatter τ ≤ 9 region.

### H12 Conclusion

H12 is supported. The absolute post-threshold balking level has more influence on a class's own served rate than the within-class step size. For a clinic seeking to understand which aspect of patient balking behavior matters most for service outcomes, the rate at which patients reject long-delay offers is more consequential than the contrast between short-delay and long-delay rejection rates.
